questions.question: Your vehicle breaks down while carrying explosives. How should you warn other drivers?

options.text: Stand on the roadway and wave your arms.
Keep the driver's side door open.

questions.explanation: When your vehicle breaks down while carrying explosives, warn other drivers with reflective triangles or electric lights. Do not use flares or other burning signals — they could cause the explosives to catch fire.

questions.question: A supervisor watching a tank being loaded must do all of the following, except:

options.text: Stay within 25 feet of the tank.
Know the hazards of the materials.

questions.explanation: A tank supervisor must stay alert, stay within 25 feet of the tank, have a clear view, and know the hazards. A chemical suit is not required.

questions.question: A person loading a tank with hazardous materials must do all of the following, except:

options.text: Stay within 10 feet of the tank.
Know the hazards of the materials.
Be authorized to move the tank.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stay within 10 feet of the tank.
questions.explanation: The supervisor must stay alert, know the hazards, be authorized to move the tank, and stay within 25 feet of the tank — not 10 feet.

questions.question: If corrosive materials leak in a trailer, how should you clean it?
questions.explanation: Wash parts of the vehicle that were exposed to corrosive materials thoroughly with water.

questions.question: Who must mark and label hazardous materials for shipping?
questions.explanation: The shipper is responsible for correctly labeling and marking hazardous materials. The driver should check that the shipper did this before the trip begins.

questions.question: Who must label hazardous materials?
questions.explanation: The shipper is responsible for packaging, marking, and labeling hazardous materials. They must also supply any needed placards.

questions.question: If a hazardous material package is too small for its label, how should it be labeled?

options.text: Tie the item with other hazardous materials and label the outside of the bundle with a paper sheet.
Attach the label to a tag that is securely attached to the package.
Mark the item with a large orange dot.
Place the item in a box with a warning label.

questions.correctAnswerText: Attach the label to a tag that is securely attached to the package.
questions.explanation: Diamond-shaped hazard warning labels must be placed on hazardous material packages. If the label does not fit on the package, attach it to a tag that is securely fastened to the package.

questions.question: If "Inhalation Hazard" is on a shipping paper, what placard should the shipper display?

options.text: Poison Gas or Poison Inhalation Hazard

questions.correctAnswerText: Poison Gas or Poison Inhalation Hazard
questions.explanation: If "Inhalation Hazard" appears on shipping papers or a package, display a "Poison Inhalation Hazard" or "Poison Gas" placard.

questions.question: If hazardous material cargo is leaking, what should the driver do?

options.text: Drive to find a phone to alert emergency personnel.
Drive to a hazardous materials cleanup facility.
Park the vehicle and contact emergency personnel.

questions.correctAnswerText: Park the vehicle and contact emergency personnel.
questions.explanation: If cargo leaks, do not drive any longer than necessary. Park the vehicle, secure the area, stay with it, and get help. Continuing to drive spreads contamination over a larger area.

questions.question: Your vehicle breaks down while carrying explosives. How should you warn other drivers?

options.text: Stand on the roadway and wave your arms.

questions.explanation: When your vehicle breaks down while carrying explosives, use reflective triangles or red electric lights to warn other drivers. Never use flares or other burning signals — they could cause the explosives to catch fire.

questions.question: How is a hazardous materials warning shown?

options.text: By wrapping the package in orange
By placing the item away from other cargo and covering it with a sign

questions.explanation: Diamond-shaped signs called placards are placed on vehicles and bulk packages. They warn drivers and others about hazardous materials.

questions.question: When loading compressed gas, the liquid discharge valves should be:
questions.explanation: Keep liquid discharge valves open when loading and unloading compressed gas tanks. Keep them closed at all other times.

questions.question: On shipping papers with both hazardous and non-hazardous materials, how can you identify the hazardous materials?
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials must be clearly identified on shipping papers that include both hazardous and non-hazardous items. They can be listed first, highlighted in a contrasting color, or marked with an "X" before the shipping description.

questions.question: When must you use a "Poison Inhalation Hazard" placard?

options.text: When transporting more than 100 pounds of the product.
When transporting more than 50 pounds of the product.
When transporting any amount of the product.
When the product is in a leaking container.

questions.correctAnswerText: When transporting any amount of the product.
questions.explanation: The "Poison Inhalation Hazard" placard and the correct hazard class placard must be displayed at all times. This applies to any amount of the material, even small quantities.

questions.question: When loading hazardous materials, which of the following should you NOT do?

options.text: Load the materials away from heat.

questions.explanation: Do not use hooks or sharp tools when loading hazardous materials. These tools can damage containers or packaging.

questions.question: How often must hazardous materials employees be trained?

options.text: At least once every three years

questions.correctAnswerText: At least once every three years
questions.explanation: Employees who work with hazardous materials must receive training and be tested at least once every three years.

questions.question: What is the only way to check tire pressure correctly?

options.text: By pushing on the tire to feel the pressure.

questions.explanation: You must check each tire at the start of every trip. A tire pressure gauge is the only effective way to measure tire pressure.

questions.question: What is the minimum fire extinguisher rating for placarded vehicles?
questions.explanation: The power unit of a placarded vehicle must have a fire extinguisher rated 10 B:C or higher by Underwriters Laboratories (UL).

questions.question: What is the minimum fire extinguisher rating for the power unit of a placarded vehicle?
questions.explanation: The power unit of a placarded vehicle must have a fire extinguisher rated 10 B:C or higher by Underwriters Laboratories (UL).

questions.question: Why can opening trailer doors during a cargo fire make the fire worse?

options.text: It allows oxygen into the trailer.
It changes the temperature of the trailer.
It provides more moisture to the trailer.

questions.correctAnswerText: It allows oxygen into the trailer.
questions.explanation: Opening trailer doors during a cargo fire is dangerous. Fresh oxygen enters the area and can cause the fire to flare up and spread quickly.

questions.question: What shape are the warning signs for hazardous materials on vehicles?
questions.explanation: Vehicles carrying hazardous materials must display diamond-shaped warning signs on all four sides. These signs are called placards.

questions.question: What must a package with liquid containers display?

options.text: Arrows pointing in the correct upright direction.
The number of containers inside the box.

questions.correctAnswerText: Arrows pointing in the correct upright direction.
questions.explanation: Packages with liquid containers must show arrows pointing in the correct upright direction. This tells handlers which way to keep the package.

questions.question: What are portable tanks?

options.text: Cannot be removed from a vehicle.
Are not permanently attached to a vehicle.
Are permanently attached to a vehicle.

questions.correctAnswerText: Are not permanently attached to a vehicle.
questions.explanation: Portable tanks are not permanently attached to a vehicle. Cargo tanks stay on a vehicle at all times, but portable tanks can be removed.

questions.question: Shippers package hazardous materials in order to ____ them.
questions.explanation: Shippers package hazardous materials to fully contain them. Vehicles must display placards to show what hazardous cargo is inside.

questions.question: Where can you find identification numbers for chemicals?

options.text: In the DOT Emergency Response Guide.
In the Periodic Table of Elements.

questions.correctAnswerText: In the DOT Emergency Response Guide.
questions.explanation: The DOT Emergency Response Guide (ERG) contains information about hazardous chemicals. It is organized by proper shipping names and identification numbers.

questions.question: How should containers of nitric acid be stacked?

options.text: Stacked no more than two containers high.
Loaded on top of other products.

questions.correctAnswerText: Stacked no more than two containers high.
questions.explanation: Nitric acid containers can be stacked, but only two containers high maximum. They should not be stacked on top of other products.

questions.question: How often must hazardous materials employees be trained and tested?
questions.explanation: Hazardous materials employees must be trained and tested at least once every three years. They must learn about the risks and how to respond to emergencies.

questions.question: What class of hazard is an explosive material?
questions.explanation: Class 1 hazardous materials include items that can explode or cause fire hazards.

questions.question: Who controls hazardous materials laws?
questions.explanation: Federal, state, and local governments all create rules for transporting hazardous materials because of the risks involved.

questions.question: Should identification numbers, shipping names, and hazard classes be abbreviated on shipping papers?

options.text: Yes, if the paper is small.
Yes, to make them easier to read.
No, they should never be abbreviated.
Yes, if the abbreviations are easy to understand.

questions.correctAnswerText: No, they should never be abbreviated.
questions.explanation: Never abbreviate identification numbers, shipping names, or hazard classes on shipping papers. The only exception is if the regulations specifically allow the abbreviation.
